name: Fight or Flight

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the moat and start in the blocky line of face holds just left of the gully/chimney that bounds the left edge of the buttress. Most of the pitch is low fifth class on clean granite; a wide crack near the top holds the harder moves. The moat at the start can be awkward and changes through the season.

Trend up and right to the top of the lingering snow patch, aiming for the clean wall beneath a shallow left-facing corner. How much snow sits here varies a lot year to year, and in a big year it can bury this ground; belay at the base of the clean wall.

Unprotected but balancy face climbing leads to the corner, which takes good gear and has had a fixed piton in it. Above the top of the crack, hard face climbing on good gear finishes at a belay ledge. The runout off the belay comes before the first solid piece, so move carefully.

Face climb left off the belay on positive holds with little protection, then pull into a steep dihedral split by twin cracks and follow clean flakes and cracks to a pedestal. Among the best pitches on the route; gear is mostly small.

Step down and left from the belay into a hidden corner, climb it, and work back up and right to belay at a spot directly above the previous stance. The corner is not visible from the pedestal, so traverse down to find it rather than forcing straight up.

Move left and up to the base of a long seam and finger crack, which protects well as the moves get harder. From its base work left and up around a series of left-facing corners and small roofs toward the left edge of the wall, belaying low beside the chimney/gully.

Climb the featured arête right of the chimney/gully, then a clean white shallow dihedral, and undercling right to the belay. Protection on the arête is sparse and relies on small cams (TCU sizes); expect a long, committing stretch that some find runout.

A strenuous left-facing corner with sustained finger locks leads on up the left side of the buttress. Above this pitch the rock turns noticeably mossier, especially in the obvious dihedrals, so avoid the corners and look for cleaner flakes and cracks.

Follow flakes and cracks left onto a bright quartz dike, which gives about two pitches of continuous positive holds with only occasional gear. From a small ledge below the summit, a hidden snow patch and a steep final rock wall with an overhanging pull-up move lead to the top; an ice tool helps if that snow is still there.

rappels: Not a rappel descent - down-climb the East Ridge and north-facing snow slopes instead
descent_text: From the top of the route, descend via Castle Peak's east ridge to an obvious col, then down a snow finger back toward the approach glacier/basin, rather than reversing the climbing line.
approach: Two approaches exist, both multi-day. The first-ascent party came from Canada: from Lightning Lake in E.C. Manning Provincial Park, about seven miles of trail over the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then cross-country south over the border, through the Princess Creek basin and into the Crow Creek drainage below Castle's north face to the toe of the north-face glacier. Walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, so that line is recorded, not recommended. The lawful approach is from the US side: boat or hike up Ross Lake from the WA-20/Ross Dam trailhead (permit from the North Cascades Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount) to Lightning Creek, then follow the Lightning Creek Trail and the abandoned, increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek Trail past the Freezeout cabin (3,600 ft), a much longer multi-day trudge. Both approaches finish by crossing the mellow north-face glacier to the base of the buttress -- watch for an awkward bergschrund/moat at the start of the route.
overview: The North Face (Left Buttress) climbs a direct line up the left margin of Castle Peak's central north buttress, roughly 1,400 ft of granite with about half the pitches rated 5.10; the route follows clean cracks and corners low on the wall, then a distinctive yellow quartz dyke higher up to avoid dirtier rock, with generally solid, clean granite throughout.
beta: Established in 2008 during an attempt to repeat the nearby 1993 Colorado Route, this line instead follows independent ground up the left side of the main north-face buttress system. It is one of at least four distinct technical lines on this face -- do not confuse it with the original 1979 Beckey-Nolting-Tindall north-face route or the 2017 'Drawbridge' (Zentler/Schilling), which climbs the central buttress directly below the summit. Rated 5.10d/6b+/E3 5b, Grade IV, with 3 stars.
gear: Trad rack to 3 inches, doubled in small-to-medium sizes
A few pitons for older fixed placements
Ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach/descent
fa: Blake Herrington and Peter Hirst, August 3, 2008 (attempting a repeat of the 1993 Colorado Route; forced left by a detached hanging snow patch into new terrain)
face: North Face, left margin of the central buttress
